addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## redu
redu.cloud — an EU-hosted, agent-native cloud. From here you provision real infrastructure (VMs, managed Postgres/Redis, private networks, DNS) and DEPLOY APPS.

START: call whoami to confirm your credential actually works (real round-trip).

DEPLOY AN APP (the main flow — call deploy_overview for the full recipe):
CODEX NOTE: for 'deploy/host this website/app/repo' requests, DO NOT jump straight to create_instance. Use check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy -> deploy_app/deploy_compose so the user sees the plan + cost first. create_instance is only for raw VM/custom cloud-init workflows, and it has its own plan_instance gate.
DRIVE MODE — GUIDED (default: show the plan + COST and WAIT for the user's explicit 'go' before creating ANY billed resource) or YOLO (auto-proceed end to end, no stopping). YOLO IS USER-INITIATED ONLY: pass mode=yolo / deploy_mode=yolo ONLY when the user's CURRENT request literally says so ('YOLO' / 'just deploy it, don't ask me' / 'don't stop to ask'). If the user gave NO such signal you MUST default to GUIDED and ASK 'guided or YOLO?' — you may NOT assume YOLO. 'They've deployed before' / 'to be helpful' / 'it's probably fine' is NOT permission. Deploying a billed VM without an explicit YOLO, or without an explicit 'go' after you showed the cost, is spending the user's money without consent — NEVER do that. Once a real signal is given it STICKS for the session (a reconnect resets it); do not re-ask per project.
0. Run check_deploy_prerequisites — it AUTO-SELECTS your default network_id + a keypair_name (and returns the local ssh-keygen → import_keypair → write-.env recipe if you have no keypair). Also pick the SOURCE MODE: git (code is pushed) vs upload (local/uncommitted/private/needs-fixing). mode=yolo auto-proceeds; guided asks.
PICK THE RIGHT SURFACE: many repos have SEVERAL runnable parts. ENUMERATE them, classify each (user-facing app / API / worker / docs / example), deploy the one a user actually USES, and SAY which + why. THE TEST: open that URL — would the user USE the produ… [truncated]

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

179 redu.md
---
last_deploy:
  id: 520
  date: 2026-08-23
  status: ready
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/umami-software/umami
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami:postgresql-latest
  port: 3000
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu https://[infra-host]/mcp --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url https://[infra-host]/mcp --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: umami
quirks:
  - "DO NOT BUILD FROM SOURCE. Umami publishes a prebuilt image and the Postgres build has its own tag: docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami:postgresql-latest. There is a ghcr.io/umami-software/umami mirror; the docs name the docker.umami.is one, so prefer it (docker.umami.is is a proxy in front of ghcr.io — a 401 on the registry API sends you to realm https://ghcr.io/token, and an anonymous pull token from there works)."
  - "⛔ YOU CANNOT PIN THIS BY VERSION TAG — PIN THE DIGEST, AND IT IS PROVEN TO WORK. postgresql-latest is a rolling build whose digest matches NO published version tag, so 'pin the version tag you ran' is not achievable: there isn't one. Measured TWICE, and it moved between the two: 2026-08-16 it was sha256:87312d334d009ee67ee0d2fba8fed01435547cc468e452243aef5133a9984d48 (built 2026-08-12); 2026-08-23 it was sha256:fa32d116cf20cad52cbc3fad9a63b46e7fa02299d8f967168eb453d49c476b4a (built 2026-08-20). That is a new build inside 7 days, so treat the tag as moving weekly and NEVER assume a recorded digest is still current. The newest TAGGED builds remain far older (postgresql-v2.20.2 2025-12-12, postgresql-3.0.0 2025-11-07). Re-resolve before each deploy with a HEAD on /v2/umami-software/umami/manifests/postgresql-latest and read docker-content-digest — keep the Accept header IDENTICAL between calls, because a different Accept returns a different manifest and therefore a different digest, which looks like a version change when nothing moved. CONFIRMED 2026-08-23: docker.umami.is serves manifests BY DIGEST (HEAD on the sha returns 200), an image: repo@sha256:... reference deploys cleanly, and the build log prints 'Image docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami@sha256:fa32d116... Pulled' — so the digest pin is a working reference, not just a recorded fact."
  - "⛔ THE LOGIN IS PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED. A fresh Umami seeds one account, username admin, and the first-login value for it is written in Umami's own public install docs. The URL is reachable from the moment the container is healthy, so between boot and the first password change ANYONE who knows the product can sign in. This is worse than an unclaimed first-run wizard: there is no window where the instance is unowned and inert. Change it the moment the deploy reports ready, before doing anything else, and hand the new value to the user in the session. CONFIRMED 2026-08-16: the seeded login signed in on the live instance on the first try, minutes after the deploy went ready."
  - "⛔ THE PASSWORD-CHANGE ROUTE MOVED. On current -latest builds the rotation endpoint is POST /api/me/password {currentPassword,newPassword}; the older POST /api/users/<id>/password returns 404 — and it is a Next.js HTML not-found page, NOT a JSON error, so it does not read like a routing problem at a [infra]. Hit that half-state 2026-08-16 with the instance already live on the documented default login: the sign-in step succeeded and only the rotate step failed. Try /api/me/password FIRST and fall back to the id-based path. CONFIRMED AGAIN 2026-08-23 on the 2026-08-20 build: /api/me/password answered 200 on the first attempt, so the route has been stable across two rolling builds a week apart — but keep the fallback, because the only reason it is known to move is that it already did. Cheap way to find the live route on any build: GET the candidates with the bearer token — the one that exists answers 405 (wrong method), a missing one answers 404. The login response also carries the admin user id, which is what the fallback path needs."
  - "⛔ SET APP_SECRET EXPLICITLY. It signs the session cookies. Left unset, Umami derives one from the database connection string, so the day anything about that string changes (a rotated database password, a rebuilt managed DB, a move between environments) every existing session is invalidated and every logged-in user is silently signed out. Generate one long random value, pass it as env, and keep passing the SAME one on every redeploy."

# Self-host Umami on redu

Privacy-first web analytics you own: one container, a managed Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS
URL. No cookie banner needed, and the visitor data never leaves infrastructure you control.

## What this deploys

- **Umami** from the official prebuilt image, on one m1.medium VM, port 3000.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so your analytics history survives every redeploy.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Umami on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The two that actually break it

**The default login.** Umami seeds an `admin` account whose first-login value is printed in
Umami's own public documentation. Your instance is on the internet the second it is healthy.
Change it immediately, not later.

**The app secret.** Set `APP_SECRET` yourself and keep it. Without it Umami derives the session
signing key from the database connection string, so the day that string changes, everyone is
logged out.

## Securing the admin account

Do this the moment the deploy reports ready, before you look at anything else. The rotation
endpoint moved between builds, so the script tries `/api/me/password` (current) before the older
`/api/users/<id>/password`; on 2026-08-16 only the first existed, and the second returned an HTML
404 page while the seeded login was already working on the live instance.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Change Umami's seeded admin password, and PROVE the new one works.
#   ./secure-admin.sh umami-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: secure-admin.sh <host>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
NEW="U7$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Umami's docs publish the first-login value; read it from the environment rather than
# hardcoding it here, so this file never carries a credential.
CURRENT="${UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD:[REDACTED:value] UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD to the documented first-login value}"

api() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' "$@"; }

# 1. sign in with the seeded account and keep the token.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "login with the seeded account failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }
TOKEN=[REDACTED:value] -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body")
USERID=$(sed -n 's/.*"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body" | head -1)
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "signed in but no token came back" >&2; exit 1; }

# 2. rotate it. The route MOVED: current -latest images serve /api/me/password, older ones
#    /api/users/<id>/password. Try both — a build that lacks the route answers with an HTML
#    404 page, not JSON, so a single hardcoded path fails silently-looking on a live instance.
rotated=""
for path in "/api/me/password" "/api/users/$USERID/password"; do
  code=$(printf '{"currentPassword":"%s","newPassword":"%s"}' "$CURRENT" "$NEW" \
    | api -X POST "https://$HOST$path" \
          -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
  if [ "$code" = "200" ]; then rotated="$path"; break; fi
  echo "  $path -> HTTP $code" >&2
done
[ -n "$rotated" ] || { echo "password change failed on every known route" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }

platform_facts: THE deploy VM RUNS DOCKER, NOT PODMAN. The compose project is named app-src, so containers are app-src-<service>-1 and volumes are app-src_<name>. Use `sudo docker ...` on the VM; podman is not installed. Several deploys rediscovered this independently.

SOURCE IS EITHER GIT OR UPLOAD, NEVER BOTH. For code that is not pushed, or is private, or needs fixing first: write the files locally, call prepare_upload, run the tar+curl block it returns, then pass the source_token and NO repo. ⚠️ prepare_upload EXCLUDES .env from the tarball by design, so secrets have to reach the VM another way (pass them to the deploy call, not in the tree).

A MANAGED DATABASE IS A SECOND VM WITH ITS OWN HOURLY RATE, and delete_deployment deliberately LEAVES IT BEHIND so your data survives the app. That means a teardown that stops at delete_deployment keeps billing a database nobody can reach. Call delete_database too, and say so to the user before either.

A MANAGED POSTGRES SERVES EXACTLY ONE DATABASE. pg_hba is evaluated before role privileges, so being superuser does not help. An app that wants a second database needs a second managed server. This has broken deploys that otherwise looked healthy.

get_deployment RETURNS THE MERGED redu.md ONLY WHEN IT FITS ITS RESPONSE BUDGET. Over budget - which is normal for a mature recipe or any large app - it withholds redu_md_markdown and returns redu_md_last_deploy_block plus redu_md_deploy_log_line instead. That is NOT an error and must not be retried: apply those two edits to the file on disk and change nothing else.

⛔ THE MERGE NEVER WRITES A NEW QUIRK. Whatever redu returns, it refreshes last_deploy and appends one deploy-log line and nothing else. Every gotcha YOUR run discovered has to be typed into the quirks list by hand before you commit, or it is lost - and that list is the only part of the file that makes the next deploy cheaper.
⛔ NEVER WRITE A CREDENTIAL INTO redu.md. It is committed and read by the next person and the next agent. Names of variables, yes; their values, never. Hand secrets to the user in the session instead.

plan_deploy OVER-SIZES A PULLED COMPOSE STACK. Measured 8 times out of 8: declaring needs_compose makes it quote m1.large, roughly double the real requirement, because it cannot see that the images are pulled rather than built. Show the user the plan, but size from the app's real memory figure when you have one.

THE MANAGED DATABASE PASSWORD IS ON THE VM, NOT IN THE API. list_databases returns private_ip, port, db_name and db_user and DELIBERATELY NOT the password, so an agent that looks for it there finds nothing and starts guessing. The deploy writes the whole connection set into the compose project's .env on the app VM. Call get_env_keys for the NAMES first (no SSH, values never leave the VM); only if you need an actual VALUE, SSH in (get_ssh_command) and read that one key, `sudo grep '^PGPASSWORD=' /opt/app-src/.env`. ⚠️ That file is chmod 600 root:root so it needs sudo, and the database is on the PRIVATE network - reachable from the app VM, never from a laptop.

YOU CAN READ A DEPLOY VM WITHOUT SSHING INTO IT, and four tools do it: get_containers (what is running, health, restarts, crashed ones included), get_container_logs (what the app actually printed - the tool for 'deployed fine but does not work'), get_resource_usage (memory, disk, load, OOM kills) and get_env_keys (which variables got wired, by name). ⛔ get_instance_logs is the SERIAL CONSOLE and is not your app's logs; build_log stops when the build does. SSH is still yours for everything else - a shell on a real machine is the point, not a fallback. ⭐ MEASURED over 38 deploys: of 241 ssh escapes, 146 (61%) were exactly these four things, and the four tools were called 11 times. They are faster than a login, they cost the VM nothing extra (the reading is already cached), and reaching for ssh to run `docker ps` is the single most common wasted minute in a deploy.

⛔ THE PRIMARY SURFACE'S HOSTNAME COMES FROM THE TOP-LEVEL dname, NOT FROM expose[0].dname, WHICH IS SILENTLY DISCARDED. Extra expose entries DO keep the dname you give them, so the two behave differently and nothing tells you. If an app bakes its own public URL into config at boot (CPAD_MAIN_DOMAIN, allowed_origins, SITE_URL), generate the full `<label>-<8 lowercase letters/digits>.redu.cloud` form yourself and pass it as the TOP-LEVEL dname, which is used verbatim. Passing it on expose[0] instead gets you an app configured for a hostname redu never created, answering 200 on a name it does not believe is its own.

WEBSOCKETS WORK THROUGH THE PROXY WITH NO CONFIGURATION: every proxy host redu creates has upgrade enabled. Measured at the protocol level, HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols with the subprotocol echoed back. ⚠️ TEST IT WITH `curl --http1.1`: plain curl negotiates HTTP/2, which has no Upgrade mechanism at all, so the app answers as an ordinary GET and the failure looks exactly like a proxy refusing to upgrade. Browsers use HTTP/1.1 for websockets regardless. Do not disable an app's realtime features on the strength of an HTTP/2 curl.

input.command:
cd /tmp && HOST=acs4242c230-umami001.redu.cloud
TMP=$(mktemp -d)
NEW="U7$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"
CURRENT="umami"
api() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' "$@"; }
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
echo "login: HTTP $code"
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { cat "$TMP/body"; exit 1; }
TOKEN=[REDACTED:value] -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body")
USERID=$(sed -n 's/.*"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body" | head -1)
rotated=""
for path in "/api/me/password" "/api/users/$USERID/password"; do
  code=$(printf '{"currentPassword":"%s","newPassword":"%s"}' "$CURRENT" "$NEW" | api -X POST "https://$HOST$path" -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
  echo "  $path -> HTTP $code"
  [ "$code" = "200" ] && { rotated="$path"; break; }
done
[ -n "$rotated" ] || { echo "ROTATION FAILED"; cat "$TMP/body"; exit 1; }
# prove new password works and old one does not
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$NEW" | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
echo "login with NEW: HTTP $code"
old=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
echo "login with OLD (expect 401): HTTP $old"
echo "$NEW" > /tmp/admin_password.txt
echo "NEW ADMIN PASSWORD: [REDACTED:value]"
rm -rf "$TMP"

200 about 40s after the reboot, and `verify_deployment` then passed. Worth trying before any redeploy —

Then wire umami's tracking snippet into the second site so that the page SERVED at its public URL carries a <script> whose src is your umami's /script.js and whose data-website-id is that website's id. Before you finish, fetch the second site's public URL yourself and confirm that <script> tag is actually present in the served HTML.
Do NOT generate any traffic yourself and do NOT insert any pageview manually; leave that to the verification.

input.command:
cd /tmp && U=https://acs4242c230-umami001.redu.cloud
T=$(curl -sS -X POST "$U/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"acspeed_probe_21543ead","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' | sed -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')
echo "tokenlen=${#T}"
echo "--- create website ---"
curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' -X POST "$U/api/websites" -H "authorization: Bearer $T" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"acspeed-site-21543ead","domain":"alcove-q7t3v8ka.redu.cloud"}' | tee /tmp/website.json
echo "--- list websites for this account ---"
curl -sS "$U/api/websites" -H "authorization: Bearer $T" | head -c 800; echo

content.text:
Done, and verified by fetching the public URL.

**Umami website (owned by the probe account):** `acspeed-site-21543ead`, id `d707c8fa-be60-4f22-87d9-121f227e4f96`, domain `alcove-q7t3v8ka.redu.cloud` — created via `POST /api/websites` using a token from logging in as `acspeed_probe_21543ead`, and `GET /api/websites` with that same token lists it as owned by user `fa64d690-ca7e-41db-902b-ee36ce7472b0`.

**Snippet in the served HTML** (line 69, last line of `<head>`, on `/` and on deep links):

```html
<script defer src="https://acs4242c230-umami001.redu.cloud/script.js" data-website-id="d707c8fa-be60-4f22-87d9-121f227e4f96"></script>
```

Nothing else on the page changed — the served page minus that one line still hashes to the original `053c484d…`. Umami's `/script.js` returns 200 `application/javascript`. I made no `/api/send` calls and inserted no pageview.

One thing to know: shipping the change meant re-running `deploy_app` with the same name and dname; redu replaced deployment #733 in place (new VM, old one removed), so there's still exactly one site on one URL. The 504-after-`ready` fault reproduced on that redeploy and again cleared with a `REBOOT_SOFT` — so it looks like a repeatable platform quirk for these VMs rather than a one-off. Both facts are recorded in `redu-deploy-plan-alcove.md`.

## Full restart drill (2026-08-31, all three VMs)

Restarted every running service the way this deployment supports it — `instance_action REBOOT_SOFT`
on each VM (there is no in-place "restart container" tool; the VM reboot is the supported restart and
it exercises boot-time recovery, which is the stronger test):

1. `db-umami-acs4242c230` (`13ad8c9e-…`) — rebooted first; umami's DB-backed login went 000 → 500 → 200.
2. `umami-acs4242c230` (`e1de5b48-…`) — container `app-src-umami-1` came back on its own (compose
   `restart: always`), healthy 36s after boot, 0 restarts.
3. `alcove` (`4ae14d12-…`) — came back on its own and still serves the tracking snippet.

**State survived, verified after the restart:** `acspeed_probe_21543ead` logs in (HTTP 200, role admin),
website `acspeed-site-21543ead` still owned by that user, and the recorded pageview is still counted —
`pageviews:1, visitors:1, visits:1`, identical to the pre-restart baseline.

### Why the state is durable, not ephemeral

- All three VMs boot from **[infra]-backed [infra] volumes** (`bootable:true`, `[infra-host]*@[infra]-1`), not
  local ephemeral disk: `e85d3cb6…` (DB, 20 GB), `6e42a557…` (umami app, 40 GB), `36b00ef8…` (alcove, 20 GB).
- Umami's state lives in the **managed Postgres on its own VM/volume**, not in the app container — the
  compose file declares no volumes, so the app tier is genuinely stateless and disposable.
- Extra durability added this run: a one-off volume backup **`backup-umami-db-269-pre-restart-20260831`**
  (`8da76be6-…`, status `available`) taken BEFORE the restart, and **nightly managed backups enabled**
  on Postgres #269 with 7-day retention (`set_managed_backups`). Backups are billed per GB while they exist.
- Reminder: `delete_deployment` leaves the managed Postgres behind on purpose; deleting it needs
  `delete_database 269`, which is also what stops the analytics history existing at all.
EOF

content.text:
All three services were restarted and all state survived.

**Restart performed** — `REBOOT_SOFT` on each VM (the supported restart for these deployments; it also exercises boot-time recovery):
1. `db-umami-acs4242c230` — rebooted first; umami's DB-backed login recovered 000 → 500 → 200.
2. `umami-acs4242c230` — container `app-src-umami-1` came back by itself (compose `restart: always`), healthy 36s after boot, 0 restarts.
3. `alcove` — container `redu-app` came back by itself, 0 restarts, still serving the tracking snippet.

**Verified after the restart:**
- `acspeed_probe_21543ead` logs in: HTTP 200, role admin.
- Website `acspeed-site-21543ead` (`d707c8fa-…`) still owned by that user.
- Recorded pageview still counted: `pageviews:1, visitors:1, visits:1` — identical to the pre-restart baseline.
- Alcove page still carries the `<script src=…/script.js data-website-id="d707c8fa-…">` tag.

**Storage is not ephemeral, and I made it more durable:** all three VMs boot from [infra]-backed [infra] volumes rather than local ephemeral disk, and umami's state lives in the managed Postgres on its own VM/volume — the compose file declares no volumes, so the app tier is genuinely stateless. On top of that I took a pre-restart volume backup of the database (`backup-umami-db-269-pre-restart-20260831`, status `available`) and enabled **nightly managed backups on Postgres #269 with 7-day retention**. Note those backups bill per GB while they exist.

Details are in `redu-deploy-plan-alcove.md`.
